title: Who may come to the Christian mysteries
source_text: Καὶ διδάσκοντες „ὅτι εἰς κακότεχνον ψυχὴν οὐκ εἰσελεύσεται σοφία οὐδὲ κατοικήσει ἐν σώματι κατάχρεῳ ἁμαρτίας“ φαμέν· ὅστις χεῖρας καθαρὸς καὶ διὰ τοῦτ᾿ ἐπαίρων „χεῖρας ὁσίους“ τῷ θεῷ καὶ παρὰ τὸ διηρμένα καὶ οὐράνια ἐπιτελεῖν δύναται λέγειν· „ἔπαρσις τῶν χειρῶν μου θυσία ἑσπερινὴ“, ἡκέτω πρὸς ἡμᾶς· καὶ οστις φωνὴν συνετὸς τῷ μελετᾶν τὸν νόμον κυρίου „ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς“ καὶ τῷ „διὰ τὴν ἕξιν τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα“ ἐσχηκέναι „πρὸς διάκρισιν καλοῦ τε καὶ κακοῦ“ μὴ ὀκνείτω προσιέναι στερεαῖς λογικαῖς τροφαῖς καὶ ἁρμοζούσαις ἀθληταῖς εὐσεβείας καὶ πάσης ἀρετῆς, ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ „ἡ χάρις“ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστι „μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ ἀγαπώντων“ τὸν διδάσκαλον τῶν τῆς ἀθανασίας μαθημάτων, ὅστις ἁγνὸς οὐ μόνον ἀπὸ παντὸς μύσους ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἐλαττόνων εἶναι νομιζομένων ἁμαρτημάτων, θαῤῥῶν μυείσθω τὰ μόνοις ἁγίοις καὶ καθαροῖς εὐλόγως παραδιδόμενα μυστήρια τῆς κατὰ Ἰησοῦν θεοσεβείας, ὁ μὲν οὖν Κέλσου μύστης φησίν· ὅτῳ οὐδὲν ἡ ψυχὴ σύνοιδε κακὸν, ἡκέτω· ὁ δὲ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν μυσταγωγῶν τῷ θεῷ τοῖς κεκαθαρμένοις τὴν ψυχὴν ἐρεῖ· ὅτῳ πολλῷ χρόνῳ ἡ ψυχὴ οὐδὲν σύνοιδε κακὸν, καὶ μάλιστα ἀφ᾿ οὗ προσελήλυθε τῇ τοῦ λόγου θεραπείᾳ, οὗτος καὶ τῶν κατ᾿ ἰδίαν λελαλημένων ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῖς γνησίοις μαθηταῖς ἀκουέτω, οὐκοῦν καὶ ἐν οἷς ἀντιπαρατίθησι τὰ τῶν μυούντων ἐν Ἕλλησι τοῖς διδάσκουσι τὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ οὐκ οἶδε διαφορὰν καλουμένων ἐπὶ μὲν θεραπείαν φαύλων ἐπὶ δὲ τὰ μυστικώτερα τῶν ἤδη καθαρωτάτων.
pass_a_gloss: And teaching that into an evil-scheming (κακότεχνος) soul wisdom will not enter (εἰσέρχομαι) nor dwell (κατοικέω) in a body indebted (κατάχρεως) to sin (ἁμαρτία), we say: whoever [is] pure of hands and for this lifting up (ἐπαίρω) holy (ὅσιος) hands to God, and through (παρά + art. inf.) performing (ἐπιτελέω) lifted-up (διαίρω, pf. pass.) and heavenly (οὐράνιος) things is able to say ‘the lifting up (ἔπαρσις) of my hands [is] an evening (ἑσπερινός) sacrifice (θυσία)’, let him come (ἥκω) to us; and whoever [is] intelligent of voice by meditating on (μελετάω) the law (νόμος) of the Lord day and night, and by having had ‘through habit (ἕξις) the faculties (αἰσθητήριον) exercised (γυμνάζω) for discernment (διάκρισις) of good and evil’, let him not hesitate (ὀκνέω) to approach (πρόσειμι) solid (στερεός) rational (λογικός) foods (τροφή) fitting (ἁρμόζω) for athletes (ἀθλητής) of piety (εὐσέβεια) and every virtue. And since also ‘the grace (χάρις)’ of God is ‘with all those loving in incorruption (ἀφθαρσία)’ the teacher (διδάσκαλος) of the lessons (μάθημα) of immortality (ἀθανασία), whoever [is] holy not only from every defilement (μύσος) but also from those thought (νομίζω) to be lesser (ἐλάττων) sins, let him, being confident (θαρρέω), be initiated (μυέω) into the mysteries (μυστήριον) of the worship of God (θεοσέβεια) according to Jesus, handed on (παραδίδωμι) reasonably (εὐλόγως) to the holy (ἅγιος) and pure (καθαρός) alone. Celsus’s initiate (μύστης) then says: ‘whose soul is conscious of nothing evil, let him come’; but the one initiating (μυσταγωγέω) to God according to Jesus will say to those purified (καθαίρω) in soul: ‘whose soul for a long time (πολλῷ χρόνῳ) is conscious of nothing evil, and especially since he came to the healing (θεραπεία) of the Word, let this one hear also the things spoken privately (κατ᾿ ἰδίαν) by Jesus to the genuine (γνήσιος) disciples (μαθητής)’. Therefore also in what he compares (ἀντιπαρατίθημι), the [practices] of those initiating among the Greeks to those teaching the [things] of Jesus, he does not know the difference (διαφορά) of the base (φαῦλος) being called to healing and of those already most pure to the more mystical things (μυστικώτερα).
pass_b_english: And since we teach that “wisdom will not enter a soul that plots evil, nor dwell in a body in debt to sin” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4), we say: Whoever has clean hands, and for that reason lifts up “holy hands” (1 Timothy 2:8) to God, and, because he performs lofty and heavenly deeds, can say, “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 141:2), let him come to us. And whoever has intelligent speech, because he meditates on the law of the Lord “day and night” (Psalm 1:2), and because he has “faculties trained by practice to distinguish good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14), let him not hesitate to come to solid food for the mind (Hebrews 5:14), food fit for athletes of piety and of every virtue.

And since “the grace” of God is “with all who love” the Teacher of the lessons of immortality “in incorruption” (Ephesians 6:24), whoever is pure not only from every defilement but also from the sins that are thought to be lesser, let him with confidence be initiated into the mysteries of the worship of God taught by Jesus, mysteries that are rightly handed on only to the holy and pure.

Celsus’s man of the mysteries, then, says: “Let him come whose soul is conscious of no evil.” But the one who, following Jesus, leads initiates to God will say to those who have been purified in soul: He whose soul has for a long time been conscious of no evil, and especially since he came to the healing of the Word, let him hear also the things that Jesus spoke in private to his true disciples (compare Mark 4:34). So, in setting the practice of those who initiate people among the Greeks against those who teach the doctrine of Jesus, Celsus does not know the difference between the wicked, who are called to healing, and those already most pure, who are called to the deeper mysteries.

choices.choice: Origen reworks each clause of the pagan proclamations quoted in 3.59 into a Christian one; his own proclamations are given as direct speech without quotation marks, so that double quotation marks stay with Celsus and with Scripture. Wisdom of Solomon 1:4 is quoted exactly. 1 Timothy 2:8 (ἐπαίροντας ὁσίους χεῖρας). Psalm 140:2 LXX = Psalm 141:2 in English Bibles. Psalm 1:2 has the same number in LXX and English. Hebrews 5:14 is quoted (διὰ τὴν ἕξιν τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα … πρὸς διάκρισιν καλοῦ τε καὶ κακοῦ), and στερεαῖς … τροφαῖς takes up ἡ στερεὰ τροφή of the same verse; both are cited. Ephesians 6:24 reads ‘with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption’; Origen puts ‘the Teacher of the lessons of immortality’ in place of the name, so ‘Teacher’ is capitalised as Christ. λογικαῖς τροφαῖς rendered ‘food for the mind’ (λογικός also carries a hint of the Logos). παρὰ τὸ διηρμένα καὶ οὐράνια ἐπιτελεῖν: διηρμένα (‘lifted up’) rendered ‘lofty’. ὁ Κέλσου μύστης: μύστης is usually ‘initiate’, but here it is the one making the proclamation; rendered ‘Celsus’s man of the mysteries’, set against ὁ μυσταγωγῶν (‘the one who leads initiates’). τῶν κατ᾿ ἰδίαν λελαλημένων ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῖς γνησίοις μαθηταῖς alludes to Mark 4:34 (κατ᾿ ἰδίαν δὲ τοῖς ἰδίοις μαθηταῖς), cited with ‘compare’. οστις in the staged text = ὅστις.

Checked: Wisdom of Solomon 1:4 exact; 1 Timothy 2:8; Psalm 140:2 LXX = Psalm 141:2; Psalm 1:2; Hebrews 5:14 (both the trained faculties and solid food); Ephesians 6:24 (‘in incorruption’); Mark 4:34 (κατ᾿ ἰδίαν … μαθηταῖς) as an allusion
